title: The Difference Between Fact, Opinion, and Truth
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece draws sharp definitional lines between three concepts leaders routinely conflate: facts (objectively verifiable and unchanged by belief), opinions (value judgments that may or may not rest on facts, and can shift quickly), and truths (shared beliefs people choose to hold, which don't require logical proof). The article argues these three forces are frequently at war for influence over how people interpret social and organizational issues, and that smart leaders deliberately weight fact-grounded opinions and truths more heavily than ideologically-driven ones. It closes by calling the denial of facts to support a preferred view both irrational and disingenuous.
points: Facts, opinions, and truth are given precise, non-overlapping definitions — facts are objectively verifiable, opinions are value judgments, truths are shared beliefs that don't require proof.
The piece argues these three forces are "often at war" for influence over how people interpret contested issues, making the distinction practically useful, not just academic.
Smart leaders are urged to give more credibility to opinions and truths that are grounded in facts, rather than in prevailing ideology.
Denying facts to preserve a preferred conclusion is characterized bluntly as both irrational and disingenuous.
quotes: A fact is indisputable. Facts can be objectively verified and proven through evidence.
Opinions, on the hand, are value judgments that expresses a feeling or view. They may or may not be supported by facts.
Truth is created by people to describe how things really are. They are best described as a state of belief that is thought to represent a universal reality.
Facts, opinions, and truth are often at war with each other. They vie for influence over how people think about a given issue or topic.
Denying facts in support of a view is not only irrational, but disingenuous.
Great leaders form solid opinions and make quality decisions based on facts. That’s the truth.
